title: Light poured out
hook: sunlight seems poured down but is never used up (Meditations 8.57)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fountain, the spring that keeps rising. Your line was the spring runs clear.

Sit in a room with one window on a sunny afternoon and watch the patch of light on the floor. It's been pouring in all day, more every minute, and the window never runs dry. The sun never sends a bill. Nobody has to refill it. In book eight of his Meditations, Marcus noticed the same plain thing, sunlight coming in, and found in it a picture of how a mind should move through the world.
screen: `A PATCH OF LIGHT ON THE FLOOR.` → `POURING IN ALL DAY.` → `LIGHT POURED OUT.`

segments.voice: The sun's light seems poured down, Marcus says, spread out in every direction, and yet it isn't poured away. It isn't used up. The spreading is a kind of stretching out. Then a word game. The Greek word for rays is aktines, and Marcus says they're called that from a verb meaning to be stretched out. It's his own word play; the point isn't the dictionary but the picture: light reaches out without leaving its source. Next, watch sunlight come through a narrow opening into a dark house. It travels in a straight line, and when it meets something solid that blocks it, it rests there. It doesn't slide off or fall. It just lights up what's in front of it. That's how Marcus wants his own mind to pour itself out: not emptied, not crashing violently into whatever stands in the way, but resting on it, lighting whatever will take the light. And if something refuses it, he says, that thing only deprives itself. So attention, warmth, effort, given like sunlight, can reach far and still not run out, as long as they're poured, not thrown.
screen: `POURED DOWN, NEVER USED UP.` · `AKTINES: MARCUS'S WORD PLAY.` · `THE BEAM RESTS ON WHAT IT MEETS.` · `A MIND THAT POURS, NOT CRASHES.` · then, large: `POURED OUT.`

segments.voice: If you can, move into sunlight, a window or a patch on the floor; if it's night, picture one. Let it rest on your hands, and notice that it doesn't push or rush; it just arrives and stays. Then think of one person you'll see today, and imagine your attention reaching them like that, steady and warm, not forcing, not running out.
Aktines. Marcus's Greek word for the sun's rays: stretched out in every direction, never used up, resting on what they meet. Today's word.
Your line: poured out. Light rests on what it meets, and isn't used up. Day six hundred four, done.

original.note: Greek: a ray of light (plural aktines). Marcus links it, playfully, to a verb meaning to stretch out.

what a scholar hears: Marcus ties aktis, a ray, to ekteinesthai, to be stretched out, and makes the word play carry his point: light is extension, not loss.

notes: 8.57 paraphrased: the sun appears poured down and diffused but not effused; diffusion is extension; aktines named from ekteinesthai; light through a narrow opening into a dark room goes straight and rests on a solid body; so should the mind's outpouring be, not violent, illuminating what receives it; what does not admit it deprives itself. Confirm.
Confirm that the aktis/ekteinesthai derivation is not accepted by standard lexicons (it is generally treated as Marcus's own etymology).
